p: We would not. Okay. We are— in our proposal, we would not.
I wanna go to a different line of questioning.
Not for TPT.
Not for TPT but they would absolutely be prioritized for some of our other enforcement programs. This is a limited program in that way.

So I wanna talk about the tenant ownership model here. Um, the tenant ownership model seems very weak to me, it doesn't allow— I, I've worked on TPT buildings that still haven't moved to tenant ownership, you know, 30 years later. I'm wondering how can we guarantee that tenants who are, who are agreeing to do this will, will at the end, as long as they comply with the obligations that they have, ensure that those tenants will move into an ownership model?
Um, sure, thank you for that question. Um, we are happy to support in this new legislation the opportunity for HDFC co-ops

Not HDFCs, I'm talking about buildings that are in TPT that we want them to become tenant ownership buildings, that those buildings will actually guarantee to be transitioned to tenant ownership. Because right now you're transferring it to a third party with no guarantee, even if the tenants comply, that those units will be turned over to the tenants as, as a cooperative.

So there's, there's a few places that we're supporting tenant ownership. That is allowing HDFC co-ops to reconstitute, as well as providing the opportunity for buildings that are rentals to be able to petition in. The buildings must first and foremost meet the minimum eligibility criteria to petition. We will provide notifications to these buildings to let them know what that criteria is.
What guarantees tenants the ability to get their buildings if they agree with a go-to-with-a-third-party transfer to ensure those buildings become ownership buildings?
Tenants must meet— the building must meet the eligibility criteria.
So they meet those criteria. What guarantees did HPD put into place to ensure those buildings will become tenant ownership?
Part of
They’re criteria. We're going— we have clear criteria for the standards that they have to meet.
So if tenants comply, what—

And these are based in part on some of our experiences with the past, with some of the very buildings that you've struggled with. We know that if tenants are going to take over some of these formerly very troubled buildings, they have to be set up for success. So we have, uh, from this work that we've been doing, worked to identify what is it that's going to really set every one of those tenants up to be successful in that building, and that's the starting point here. And that's where HPD can promise you that when we're working with these buildings, if they can meet that criteria, that we're gonna help them— be able to help them get into that ownership.

Why not just do a, a process where they go into tenant ownership as they meet those criteria instead of having a third party who can hold it up for 20 years to ensure as long as they meet their criteria, they're doing their classes, they're doing their training, they can have a third-party monitor to oversee them. Why not, why not give tenants the power to have ownership as an opportunity to guarantee that they will be able to move those buildings into ownership instead of

saying, tenants, you're gonna have to do this work, but then you're gonna have to rely on this third party to agree to transfer them, and there's no guarantee HPD or anyone else can force them to turn it over to you.

We don't anticipate that this is going to take 20 years. We believe if the tenants are well set up, we will be able to facilitate these transactions. But these are incredibly troubled buildings. We've been testifying to the fact that they are the worst of the worst. It does mean that we owe it to those tenants to make sure that, that building is ready. We're devoting lots of resources, including through the Owner Resource Center, um, through other parts of HPD, to make sure that we are working with everyone involved to make this program really successful. We'd be happy to offline with you about particular buildings that you're concerned about, but we do believe that the combination of factors, both the resources that the agencies are putting towards this, the standards that we've set out for tenants to be successful, and our general interest in supporting

this means that we are going to be able to do this and better than we've done it in the past.

I, I, I just— it sounds like there's no guarantee that tenants will have, if they commit to doing all their trainings and following through everything, that they can guarantee through this process legislatively to get ownership of the building and you're saying you're gonna provide resources, and you're saying there a trouble building. I know, I, I represented many of these buildings in my career to help people become tenant ownership. To then have a nonprofit refuse 5 years later, 10 years later, to even sell the building to the tenants, which leaves the tenants extremely frustrated. So I wanna hear why we— what can we do to guarantee these tenants tenant ownership?

We're, we're gonna be providing clearer timelines and milestones for achieving tenant ownership. We know we've had buildings in the past where there have been timing issues. Part of, uh, what we'll be providing programmatically is ensuring that we have those clear timelines laid out so both

the tenants and the owners and HPD understand what milestones they have to reach for tenant ownership.
Why couldn't we do that statutorily then instead of just waiting to have you through rulemaking create those timelines?

We could talk more about what you're looking for in terms of what that would look like. Um, we don't see this as a lack of guarantee. We see this as we are going to map out the program and make sure that it works for everyone, and we're happy to offline on some of these details if it doesn't seem like it's going to achieve what you're looking for.

Thank you. No, and I was just to, to follow up on Council Member Epstein. If, if I understand you correctly, um, and, and please cut me off if I'm not, um, it, it does seem like HPD does have criteria that tenants are— need to, to go through and, and, you know, many hoops to jump in order to become a cooperative. But then at the end, even if they've met all of these criteria, it's still up to HPD's discretion whether or not to accept those criteria, or at least that's, that's how it, that's how it comes across. And so I, I think we're asking

for clarity, and I, and I join, uh, Council Member Epstein in wanting that clarity. Would you—

Yeah, and either HPD or the, the third-party transfer designee have a lot of freedom to make some decisions that could— they, they could say to the tenants, we're— even though you've met these criteria, we're not transferring the building. And so that leaves the tenants kind of at a lurch when they've done everything they were asked to do. We want to make sure if they've struggled, they've suffered, we're telling them there's going to be this co-op at end, um, we want some guarantees along the way that that'll actually happen, that's committed to in the law so they can rely on it. And then if they can't— if that doesn't happen, they can have a basis to sue because they've done everything they need to do because they can't just beg for it. They need— we wanna give tenants power to do the right thing here. And I'm worried that the way the process is, is gonna just reiterate the problems we had in the '90s and the early 2000s where people wouldn't get those buildings become tenant ownership

because either HPD decided or the nonprofit decided that was not gonna happen.

Yeah, I think I— we can definitely offline a little to talk a little bit more about what, uh, um, what that might look like. Um, and I'll also just say that, like, again, we— a lot of this is about removing the discretion and putting in more objective criteria. So I actually think that that maybe, um, you know, once we can talk a little bit about more what we propose, we may actually be more in alignment than as, uh, as, you know, as it seems right now, um, because that clarity, that transparency, and the additional resources, um, you know, of the objective criteria for petitioning to become tenant-owned, uh, a tenant-owned building, um, I think is, is more in line with maybe what you're envisioning now, um, and so let's talk more about it. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. I'll now turn it to Council Member Salaam.

Thank you, Chair and, um, many of the, uh, questions that were raised, of course, embodies many of our— many of our districts.

And so once, uh, that offline conversation happens, definitely we wanna make sure that we have the, um, the insight into how we move forward. Many longtime Black and brown homeowners in Harlem, particularly seniors on fixed income, reported never receiving adequate notice before Ground X. Beyond mailing a notice— what— with a tax bill, rather, what concrete multilingual and multimodal outreach will DOF implement to make these homeowners actually understand that they are at risk?

Thank you for that question. Um, during the tax lien, we, we implemented a lot of, um, new outreach models to reach tenants and would re— work to do the same with TPT. We worked with our partners at HPD, DEP, the Mayor's Public Engagement Unit, a neighborhood— a neighborhood nonprofit, er, ah, groups. We had, um, 66 different events where Council Members joined us and our partners at PEU and HPD and DEP also joined us. We developed a 2-page fact— fact sheet outlining important information about the sale, which we would do for the TPT program, um, which was available, um, to— in 10 languages and was used by the city— by all the city agencies, the Center for

Neighborhood Partnership, the outreach partners, and elected officials. We also, um, engaged with, um, person-to-person where, um, the neighborhood went— actually went— did canvass the neighborhood to let, let, um, the owners know that their property was part of the lien sale. We'd also do that same engagement with the TPT, um, program.

And can you, can you walk us through what the new 20th percentile distress threshold looks like for typical Harlem brownstone owners with modest tax debt, so, and no serious violations, and confirm they cannot be put into this program?

Thank you for that question. So, um, there's two, I think, pieces to that response. Um, many of those folks will fall under some of the exclusions that we've talked about. Um, that's a part of the legislation that the Council and HPD need to still sort of work out, but generally, uh, are quite aligned around. Um, both, uh, ensuring that, uh, folks who are living in their homes, who meet income eligibility criteria, who, um, you know, are, are,

uh, veterans or older adults or have disabilities would be excluded outright. Um, but beyond that, uh, the changes from, uh, statutory distressed to critical eligible, um, are and introducing the balanced model really are also meant to address all of those concerns from the last program. Um, we do believe that, uh, we're gonna be, ah, seeing larger buildings that are going to be, ah, meet the critical eligible definition than under statutory distress. Um, and they're going to be much more distressed, both in terms of having, ah, the physical and the financial, ah, distress and the, I mentioned that they'd be larger, but the median building size we really do expect to be, um, something like 30 units a building, not some of the smaller buildings we saw. And the block pickup removal is also really critical to that. What we saw the last time is that a lot of folks, because they were on the block— on a block with other buildings that were quite distressed, um, if they otherwise met the minimum eligibility requirements, could, uh, could be included. Um, and that's, uh, not going to hap— we're not gonna have pickup under this version.

What targeted outreach and technical assistance is HPD providing to landlords in high-poverty communities of color before they reach the distress threshold so TPT is truly a last resort and not the first response?

Sure. Um, thank you for that question. So in terms of, um, properties that are identified, uh, for the tax lien sale or removed for the tax lien sale because they've met the eligibility criteria, we're providing additional resources for those owners to understand, uh, what's available to them to have them removed from the lien sale. We're establishing and recommending an agency liaison as well as support for our owner's resource center. The owner's resource center will provide technical assistance as well as guidance on resources to how owners can remove their buildings from the tax lien sale. Um, our additional notifications will have more information both about the status of the building, the conditions that are placing them in the tax lien sale or making their— excuse me, making their buildings vulnerable for in rem foreclosure, and adding additional notifications both in statute and

programmatically so owners understand, um, all owners understand where their buildings are and how they can remove them and what resources they have access to, to be removed, um, from the in-rem process.

And Chair, if I may, just one last one. Mhm. Once a distressed property in Harlem is transferred to a third party, what enforceable guarantees exist in the regulatory agreement to ensure current Black and brown tenants can actually afford to remain there after rehabilitation, not just that the building is technically stabilized?

Uh, for all of our programs, including TPT, these are non-displacement programs. When we are working with the designated third party to put together, um, rehab and financing plans for the building, we're looking at the rents in place as well as, um, the incomes of the tenants in place. We are not rent burdening any tenants, um, which we establish as 30% of their income for any program receiving assistance from HPD and Preservation. In particular for the TPT program, is a non-displacement program.
Thank you.

Excellent, thank you. Um, and we also have a position that is being created through the current version of the bill. It's not final. Uh, for an Ombudsman person. Can you, can you speak a little bit to the agency's position on the Ombuds person?

Um, thank you so much. Uh, so we definitely agree that customer service, um, sort of the role that the ombudsperson would play is really important. I think that's where we actually saw, um, a lot of places for improvement based on how last rounds of TPT have gone. Um, our recommendation is actually more around an agency liaison, similar type of responsibility, but instead of, ah, one person for the whole thing, it's actually one person per agency who is steeped in the— let's face it— pretty complicated, um, ways that operationalizing a tax enforcement program implicates DEP, DOF, and HPD. Um, that agency liaison would be clearly identified both on an, ah, agency website, um, so folks would know who to talk to, um, and they would be the right person to help dig deep, uh, be the contact person for customer service type issues from owners who are looking to navigate out of the

program, tenants who are wondering where they are in the process if they find out that their building is a part of TPT. So we definitely agree with the goal of this recommendation from the Council. We have a proposal that we think gets to that goal.

Okay. All right. Thank you. Whenever— whenever we're not going from some somebody has to— a private citizen has to deal with multiple agencies to solve one problem versus, uh, you know, having one person that they can go to for everything. It's, it's not quite meeting the intent of why we added that provision, but we can discuss further how we can, uh, we can get it right. Um, okay, so I, I wanna move to the surplus equity, uh, provision in the legislation. Um, the old program did not consider any remaining— any equity that might be remaining at a property at the time of transfer. Um, but there have been recent Supreme Court decisions and others that would, would point in the direction of requiring the city to consider such, ah, such equity that could remain at a property. Um, and so to that vein, the new program creates an application process by which owners can apply for any

remaining equity in their equity following a transfer. Um, can you speak to HPD's position on this proposed framework, uh, allowing owners to claim any remaining equity in their property in the event of the— of a transfer? And in past rounds of TPT, was there any instance of owners being returned any version of a surplus equity?

Um, thank you for that question. I'll, I'll answer the last piece— piece first. The current statute does not have a mechanism for, uh, making a claim of surplus equity. Um, we agree that owners should have a mechanism to be able to— first, we need the statute to comply with the Supreme Court ruling, and the owners should have the ability to recoup, um, some of their equity in certain circumstances. Um, we are doing this, uh, through provide— so owners have awareness, putting notifications, early notification in, uh, outreach to the owners, as well as adding a notification to the statute that will instruct owners about how to make that surplus equity claim.

Thank you. Um, moving to, to HDFCs, um, and I always like to start at, you know,

as I did in my testimony, like to start with the background for why the city has this power of municipal foreclosure. I think in conversations leading up to today's hearing, uh, there's been a lot of, a lot of questions about why is the city taking properties, where is this coming from, and it's very important that it is a power that we've had since 1976. And so, so tracing back that history and looking at what, you know, HDFC co-ops that we have in the city today, so many of them came from that, right? So, uh, we talked about in 1994, by 1994, uh, nearly 50,000 units were in the city's ownership, um, and 22,000 of those became HDFC cooperatives, about 1,000 buildings. Can you just give us a, a quick lay of the land of what— how many HDFC cooperatives do we have remaining in the city of New York that were transferred through this mechanism or constituted through this mechanism of third-party transfer or in rem foreclosure before it? Um, and what is the relative health of HDFCs in the city of New York? HDFC co-ops, that is.

Um, so I think we can get back to you on, like, maybe more specific numbers, which we may

not have. Um, but we— I think also the way that we're looking at this is that, um, HDFC co-ops are not separated out, um, just because they're a part of the tax class that is a larger universe. However, um, because our intent is to identify the worst of the worst, we, we're really separating it that way. Um, we do know that, um, about— in, in our— some of our statistical, uh, samples and when we've done data analysis, um, about 30%, um, of the top 500 buildings, um, were HDFC or HDFC rentals.
How many properties are 30%? You're making me do math. 30% of 500 is 5 times 3, 160, 150, 160, yeah.

This would vary, right? I think that the takeaway is that it does represent that portion, um, of the total building. It would really vary, ah, in a given year, year, but also depending on the size of the sample. Um, but we do recognize that they are, ah, you know, an important block here and something that we know the working group has put a lot of thinking into and we have with your team.

And I understand that there were 83 HDFC co-ops transferred in round 10. So this is sort of consistent with an overrepresentation of

HDFCs. Um, do we know how— You said you don't have this number today, or can you get how many HDFC co-ops remain in the City of New York?
Um, we can get that for you. We definitely have that number somewhere. I just actually don't have it right in front of me, but we'll make sure we get that for you.

Okay, got it. Um, you started to talk about this, but given this disproportionate inclusion of HDFC co-ops in previous TPT rounds and, and in this model, what is HPD's stance on how HDFC in particular should be treated in a reimagined version of the program? What unique redemption options should be available to them? What additional supports should they receive?

Uh, well, I'll just say, you know, we think that HDFCs will benefit, um, from a lot of the additional, um, outreach and notifications that we are putting in place here. Um, so, you know, I, I do think that we are— first of all, the selection and eligibility criteria is gonna change, or we are proposing that it changes such that they are not overrepresented, um, in future rounds of TPT.

Um, in addition, the supplemental notices and outreach that we are proposing as part of the reforms will absolutely benefit HDFC co-ops. Um, and so, you know, we are holding ourselves to higher standards in these reforms. Um, and we do expect that there will be, um, a higher level of touchpoints because of that, including with support from our owner resource center, which is something that didn't exist in previous rounds of TPT. Um, anything else that maybe, er, Kerry, you want to add here about that?

Sure. Um, pardon me. Uh, just to add, we are adding additional notifications, um, that will give HDFC co-ops in particular— these notifications will go to everybody, but HDFC co-ops in particular will benefit from getting earlier notifications in the process. Um, we're also standardizing our payment plan so it's clear to all owners how they can remove their properties from the action. Um, Rosa mentioned the owner's resource center. We also have additional resources to homeowners programmatically outside of DBT, outside of the tax lien sale, through the Office of the Homeowner

Advocate and through the Homeowners Help Desk, both of which were established in 2024, all to bolster support for homeowners.
Can you—

And we- oh, we know that there are struggling HDC— HDFC co-ops in the city. We have a number of programs to be able to support them so that they don't get to this place and that's also something we'd really emphasize. It's a huge part of our homeownership focus is being able to help stabilize existing homeowners where they need it.

And if previous rounds, um, uh, they were not allowed to petition to, um, become cooperative owners once again. In this round, we are actually, um, ah, putting back into statute the ability for HDFC co-ops to petition to reconstitute as co-op ownership once again, even post-TPT.

Yeah, thank you. Um, can you— you said in that in your modeling, 30% of the top 500 worst buildings were HDFC co-ops and rentals. Can you give that breakdown between how many were co-ops and how many were rentals?
It's about 20%, uh, co-ops, 10% rentals.
20% of the 30%?
Yes. These are all—
You guys going to help me out with the math?

These are all estimates, right? They are, uh, we've worked very hard on them, but we are— they are— it would be subject in any given year to a ton of variables. We want to help everyone sort of understand what we're looking at here, but we also wanna sort of avoid the perception that it would always be that. Okay. So roughly 800— ah, 800 or 100 co-ops and 50 rentals, roughly. Roughly.
With a grain of salt, please.

That's what my Excel formula would say. Okay. Okay, Thank you and I know the HDFC coalition is watching. They're submitting testimony, but I, I do welcome the opportunity to talk further about this, because HDFC co-ops were created through in rem foreclosure. How— it, it's just poetic in the, in the wrongest way for them to go through in rem foreclosure again, uh, to lose that ownership, even if they can re-petition. So, uh, welcome the

opportunity to talk more about how we can stabilize these properties. Okay, moving to Neighborhood Restore— and one second. Moving to Neighborhood Restore, can you describe the, the details of HPD's contract with Neighborhood Restore and what is the financial relationship that the city has with, uh, this entity?

Sure. Thank you for that question. Um, Neighborhood Restore is a critical partner to HPD and was formed by LISC and Enterprise, um, to support round 1 of TPT. We provide, uh, support programmatically, um, and administratively to Neighborhood Restore at the start of each round to support their administrative functions overseeing, um, the buildings as interim owner. Um, Neighborhood Restore provides, um, immediate stabilization work as soon as the properties are transferred through the in rem foreclosure process. They're doing tenant meetings, they're issuing and working with tenants on establishing rent-stabilized leases, as well as assessing emergency conditions and addressing those conditions within the building upon transfer.

Um, HPD enters into, um, uh, an agreement with Neighborhood Restore at the start of each funding round, and the relationship is, um, outlined in an MOU between Neighborhood Restore and
At the beginning of a round, you said?
We enter into an agreement, um, where we provide funding at the beginning of every round with Neighborhood Restore.
All right, thank you. Would you provide a copy of that contractual relationship— the - a copy of the contract, uh, to this Committee?
Um, we're happy to talk more about that request,yes.

Don't make us subpoena. No, I'm kidding. Okay. Um, we're, we're all friends here. Um, Okay, HPD previously testified that past transfers on occasion have been reversed. Can you share the circumstances that led to any sample reversal or sample reversals? Uh, what was the exact mechanism for reversing a transfer? Is HPD able to do this through its contract with, with Neighborhood Restore?

I'll just start by, um, thank you so much. I, I think we'll start by saying we agree that there are definitely limited circumstances and past president— precedent where, um, reversals have been necessary. Um, and moving forward, we are really striving to carve out objective bases, um, that are fiscally responsible. Um, so as I said, we are really trying to, to be more intentional about our, um, objective criteria for many, many parts of this program. Um, but, uh, you know, in previous situations, um, we recognize that, um, sometimes an owner has attempted to address issues. So there have been situations in the past where, um, we have reversed transfers, um, because, uh, you know, certain missteps along the way. Um, we don't expect that to be, um, the case moving forward because of the new criteria and much of the smoothing out of the process that we've identified, but, um, there are also objective criteria that can trigger removal of a property prior to a final judgment. Um, that's things like the validity of a lien, or maybe the city's already collected payment on all the

taxes and interest, so that can, um, uh, er, happen when there's something subject to foreclosure. Similarly, if charges are canceled, um, that is also a situation where, um, we would reverse, and, and then also, um, Uh, just a note here that, um, applications for reversal would be subject to, um, the In Rem Foreclosure Release Board, which is a body that deals with this type of situation.
What is the current status of the In Rem Foreclosure Release Board? Uh, has it been used in the past? More?

Um, so we're supportive of keeping the In Rem Foreclosure Release Board in the current statute. Um, as Rosa said, there are limited circumstances where we will work um, where reversal will take place. Um, we need to have clear and objective criteria and limit discretion. Um, one piece that we are recommending that we would like to continue discussing is that the city will need to retain discretion to reverse transfers where there's surplus equity that cannot be supported, um, by the city.
Do you have examples of when the In Rem Foreclosure Release Board has been used?
To my knowledge, we don't have any recent examples of a release from the In-Rem Foreclosure Release Board. We'd like to continue talking about that provision with the Council.
Thank you. What are estimated costs for each of your agencies to administer the program, um, in— in the— in Round 10 and moving forward to— if there is a Round 11?

Um, sure. So in terms of looking forward to a round 11, because we're still negotiating this legislation, we are happy to keep talking about what our estimates will look like once we have finalized legislation. We do know that staffing, capital, and programmatic support is critical to the success of the TPT program and ensuring we have good customer service and are able to administer the program effectively. Um, hmm for potential costs, we will need programmatic support for the owner's resource center to support Neighborhood Restore, to be able to support, um, the appraisals that we'll need to conduct to estimate surplus equity or assess surplus equity, um, as well as to make surplus value payments, um, where necessary and, and where supported.

We'll need specific staffing support as well as capital support to ensure that we have dollars to rehab, buildings that are coming through the in rem foreclosure process and being disposed to, um, or being transferred, ah, to a third-party designated entity.
Thank you. Can you, can you talk a little bit about the process that the agency imagines undertaking to determine the surplus value?

Sure. So we have two pieces of notification that will include information about the surplus equity process. Ah, first, ah, for the final warning notice that will include information to the owner, uh, making them aware that there's an opportunity to request, um, surplus equity and what that process will look like. In the statute, we are adding a notification, um, that will be sent, um, that will require a report to be sent to the owner that includes the assessment of the surplus equity. Um, this notice will also allow owners, um, an opportunity to dispute, to either make that claim or dispute the, the findings of the appraisal.
And who is conducting the appraisal?
HPD will need to contract, um, once we have final legislation in place. We need to contract with a vendor to be able to complete those as-is appraisals.

Thank you. Um, and then turning back to tenant ownership before, uh, turning it back to my colleague Council Member Epstein, um, how many buildings have, uh, successfully converted to tenant ownership via previous rounds of TPT?
Um, thank you. Yes, there are 73 tenant petition, um, properties supported through rounds 1 through 10.
And were those 73 tenant petitions completed?

Uh, 47 have converted, 13 have remained long-term rentals, and 10 buildings are pending conversion, um, and are post-construction and loan conversion and 3 properties are in construction and pre-development.

And for the properties that are long-term, the 13 properties that are long-term rentals, the ones that are— have stalled in the

process, as we've been discussing, how does HPD understand why that stalling has occurred?

In limited circumstances, we— a tenant petition is not able to successfully convert into a co-op. I don't have exact information on the, the 13 long-term rentals. I'd be happy to talk more about those and their circumstances.

Thank you. Um, so turning to, um, the process to petition for tenant ownership, um, in the TPT working group report, you all state that Neighborhood Restore HDFC works with HPD and the selected qualified third party to stabilize, engage, and plan for rehabilitation and future ownership of these properties. Can you break down for us who— what is happening at each stage? So, uh, the transfer occurs, the tenants are working with a qualified third party. Is that qualified third party then, um, the entity that also helps them transition into ownership, or can you just break down that process for us?

Sure. Um, so at the start, uh, for any building, and, and now this will include going forward HDFC co-ops, uh, the building must meet the minimum eligibility criteria to have the opportunity

to be a tenant petition, which is what we call the, the, the future co-op process. Um, that is, the building must have 10 or more units, it must be occupied, um, 50% or more, and 80% of those tenants have to indicate, um, an interest in homeownership, a— as well as identify a designated entity from our prequalified list, um, of entities. That designated entity will take the project through predevelopment, construction, and support the co-op in forming, um, after construction has completed.

And so at which— at what point, uh, does— is that final determination made that we've done predevelopment, we've done construction, um, the ten— the tenants have come together and they've met the minimum criteria, at what point does HPD then decide that the tenants can become shareholders?

Um, as I said, there are limited circumstances where, where- where we are determining that the project has not met the milestones. Um, I don't have specific details about where in that process. It is different for every co-op. We have to ensure that the co-op is being formed to be

successful. I'd be happy to follow up and talk more about instances in terms of, uh, past, past projects.
Thank you Council Member Epstein.
If there's a history of harassment, uh, in a building where findings of harassment have been determined, is that a factor at all in your determination whether a building can go through TPT?
Um, so not specifically. So again, the criteria—
That's great. Okay, not specifically and it's not in the statute, right?
No.
So if there's a long-term history of harassment, tenant's been suffering through harassment, that is not a factor currently that you'd wanna consider in whether a building can go through TPT?
Again, I think our objective criteria that we've determined here does—

Objectively, if someone's defining harassment, that's a judge determination

that is harassment. That's an objective standard, right?

Yes, but we do have, um, lots of preservation programs and support for buildings that may not meet the criteria of TPT. We do expect that buildings that are in physical and financial distress excuse me, distress, um, may fall into that category and be captured by this program.
